Emittance serves as a crucial metric for characterizing the quality of a particle accelerator beam. While first-hand reduction in transverse emittance is a well-established technique, another approach involving the deliberate degradation of this emittance is often employed elsewhere in the machine to balance overall performance. In contrast, longitudinal emittance has historically been treated as an unaltered quantity. This study reports the pioneering experimental realization of transferring both transverse and longitudinal emittance, specifically by injecting a focused beam from an electron linac into an existing accelerator ring. Utilizing this novel method, the ring successfully achieved a record-low transverse emittance of 0.119 π mr adians, representing an 18-fold improvement.

This paper introduces a new approach for trajectory prediction in social driving scenarios, designed to enhance both computational efficiency and accuracy. To boost efficiency, we employ an asynchronous, sliding window strategy that enables the model to generate multiple future trajectories for the current instant. To improve prediction quality, we develop a Time-Saware Sequential CVAE (TSCNet) that refines each output by dynamically re-evaluating it based on the anticipated future paths. This re-evaluation process involves a Time-aware Evaluation (TAIE) module, which generates an improved TAIE (TE) score to better capture the non-linear dynamics within driving behaviors. Extensive testing on two prominent datasets, Stoa and ETH/UCY, confirms that TSCNet significantly surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods in both performance metrics and efficiency benchmarks.

The training of deep Boltzmann machines (DBMs) is notoriously difficult, often getting trapped in poor local optima that result in suboptimal performance. Although several heuristics exist to mitigate these outcomes, a systematic approach to improving DBM training remains elusive. In this work, we examine the relationship between the complexity of an optimal solution and the likelihood of successful learning within specific DBM architectures. Utilizing recent theoretical insights, we demonstrate that an information-theoretic measure derived from the partition function can effectively predict whether a particular model and training procedure will succeed. Furthermore, we establish that this measure also correlates with the optimal solution's complexity, suggesting it may guide the design of better-performing models by helping practitioners select appropriate levels of complexity. Finally, numerical experiments on a binary image classification task confirm that this complexty predictor aligns well with the model's actual learning performance.

With the advent of high-performance computing and advances in swarm intelligence, managing groups of hundreds or thousands of robots has become feasible. While recent research has largely focused on the algorithms governing these decentralized decision-making processes, there is growing interest in the human-machine interface, specifically how people can effectively direct decentralized swarms. This study introduces a sequential hand gesture recognition algorithm designed to enable natural human-swarm interaction, where users control a robot swarm by performing a series of gestures. To validate this concept, researchers developed a gesture-driven framework for a "forbidden zone" task, allowing users to define prohibited areas and have robots actively avoid them. Experiments conducted with 16 robots demonstrated the algorithm's capability to generate stable, collision-free robot formations based on hand gestures. Furthermore, physical trials involving 20 human participants revealed that 88% successfully completed the task, producing 82% gesture accuracy and 75% user satisfaction. These findings underscore the potential of hand gesture recognition as a viable, accessible, and user-friendly method for interacting with decentralized robot groups.

Automating the White Blood Cell (WBC) count process is vital for the diagnosis and treatment of various diseases. While current deep learning approaches for this task are often restricted by their dependence on specific data sources, this work presents three merged models that achieve an accuracy of 96.12% on the CBIZ dataset by utilizing a training strategy that integrates multiple diverse models. This method synthesizes outputs from a U-Net architecture, a ResNet50 variant employing center crop extraction, and a MobileNetV2 implementation utilizing random cropping.

Counterdiabatic (CD) protocols are powerful tools for rapidly preparing ground states, yet the practicality of initializing the static CD state of the one-dimensional Hubbard model has remained uncertain due to the infinite nature of its series expansion. We demonstrate that starting from the adiabatic CD term using just two fermionic operators per site allows us to reach the exact nonintegrable time-dependent CD Hamiltonian within a two-parameter family of variational terms. Remarkably, this optimized counterdiabatic drive closely approximates the integrable linear hopping model, facilitating the real-time application of the Bethe ansatz. Consequently, this method offers an exact, numerically efficient pathway to initialize the Hubbard model's ground state.

Laser-plasma interactions offer an alternative route to photon-photon collisions by generating high-density photon ensembles with tailored properties. This paper introduces a comprehensive laser-plasma framework designed to explore the regime of photon-photon physics through specifically engineered plasma environments. We provide a detailed analysis of planar laser wakefield waves, examining their radiation spectra and the resulting conditions for significant photon-photon interaction probabilities. Furthermore, we outline strategies to produce compact plasma configurations that facilitate observable photon-photon phenomena at current laser facilities.

This paper examines the sensitivity of the 2HDM framework, specifically focusing on the soft $Z_2$ breaking parameter, $m_{12}$. We establish a $Z_2$ symmetric Higgs sector where the symmetry is softly violated, resulting in a mass spectrum that includes charged Higgs bosons, a CP-even scalar, and a pseudo-scalar. By analyzing the sensitivity matrix, we determine the dependence of the Higgs boson mass, $m_h$, on $m_{12}$, revealing that this relationship is non-linear. Furthermore, we investigate how $m_{12}$ affects Higgs production and decay rates, observing that these effects are linearly dependent on $m_{12}$ for small values but become non-linear as the parameter increases. We also assess the sensitivity of the charged Higgs boson mass, $m_h^{\pm}$, to $m_{12}$, finding it to be linear for small values but non-linear for larger magnitudes. Additionally, we discuss the constraints on $m_{12}$ derived from Higgs mass and coupling measurements, as well as the impact of this parameter on the stability of the Higgs potential.

While Relational To RDF (R2RDF) mappings are typically modeled using shape expressions, existing frameworks often fail to accommodate relational data sources that already include shape definitions for objects within the table's column types. This absence of support limits the expressiveness of current mapping tools. To resolve this, our work extends existing mapping frameworks to handle RDF transformation from relational schemas alongside a separate shape expressions schema for column types. Our extension further introduces mechanisms for resolving circular type references and managing the optional nature based on shape definitions for objects stored within table columns. To address performance concerns, we developed an optimization that avoids redundant processing of the same table multiple times. Finally, we evaluated the system's performance characteristics and scalability.

This work introduces `pyStoNED`, an open-source, well-documented Python library designed for model specification, estimation, and inference of heterogeneous panel data models featuring convexity constraints. The package's utility is demonstrated through its application to a well-known local production function dataset.

Numerous research studies have focused on inverse text normalization (ITN) by employing data-driven approaches. While these methods have yielded encouraging outcomes, they frequently encounter difficulties with specific numerical formats, such as phone lists and other specialized types of structured data. This study investigates data augmentation to bolster the ITN data-driven pipeline. We propose a straightforward augmentation technique that leverages available resources to synthesize additional samples for difficult cases, thereby refining model performance. The experiments indicate that using augmented datasets rather than only clean training samples significantly enhances accuracy on these challenging instances. Furthermore, this cost-free strategy produces superior results compared to approaches that solely rely on unsupervised pre-training.

Kernel methods serve as a robust framework for conducting kernel ridge regression and support vector machines. A key challenge in designing kernels is finding a way to measure similarity between objects. This is typically achieved by defining kernels based on their respective tangents, which function as probability distributions over those objects. While existing literature has primarily developed symmetric and non-identical tangent kernels, this paper introduces an alternative class: NFT-Kernel. Unlike its predecessors, NFT-Kernels are designed to be non-identical, offering greater flexibility. The proposed method constructs a valid kernel as a convex combination of squared-softmax functions, where each function corresponds to an NFT-Kernel. The resulting NFT-Kernel can seamlessly integrate with various kernel methods, such as ridge regression and SVMs. The following sections will provide a description of this new kernel, illustrate its construction through concrete examples, and demonstrate its effectiveness in real-world machine learning tasks.

While non-Hermitian topological phases have been extensively studied in one-dimensional (1D) systems lacking correlations, understanding the impact of correlated interactions on non-trivial phases remains limited. This work examines correlated dissipation within a non-Hermitian Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model to determine how interactions diminish point-gap (PG) topology. We identify two distinct correlation regimes: an asymmetric interaction regime that retains the PG, and a symmetric interaction regime that destroys the PG. This transition is attributed to the shift in the complex many-body energy spectrum from linearity to nonlinearity, thereby disrupting the spectral condition necessary for PG stability. Furthermore, by investigating the relationship between 1D PG and 1D line-graph (LG) topology driven by correlations, we observe that while the correlation-induced destruction of bulk PGs invariably breaks line-graph topology, line-graph topology can also be severed by other mechanisms unrelated to the loss of linearity in the energy spectrum.

We examine the synthesis of social speaker traits into speech generated for specific targets, specifically exploring how these traits can be embedded into the acoustic characteristics of a newly created voice. Our work investigates two main areas: (i) introducing a methodology to embed traits into synthetic speech for a fresh speaker, and (ii) developing a metric for evaluating their retention during such transformation. Additionally, we present two novel datasets for cross-language trait transfer tasks and conduct comprehensive analyses of their performance.

We introduce a radiative seesaw framework featuring a $U(1)_{B-L}$ extension, where modular $\text{A}_4$ symmetry, combined with a $U(1)_R$ anomaly-free condition, ensures the emergence of neutrino mass phenomena. Within this framework, a $U(1)_{B-L}$ gauge interaction, which spontaneously breaks to yield a $Z'$ boson, enables both normal and inverse seesaw scenarios. Additionally, the model incorporates a dark matter candidate as the dark sector's sole resident, with its relic density determined through interactions with $Z'$ bosons and the Higgs particle.

The influence of the minimum length on collective dynamics in triaxial nuclei is examined through a Bohr-Landau Hamiltonian framework. A potential term is incorporated to trigger shape transitions, and triaxial nuclear deformations are modeled using three distinct parameters: $\gamma = 20^{\circ}, 30^{\circ},$ and $40^{\circ}$. Quantum corrections arising from the minimal length concept are analyzed within the context of the noncommutative spatial framework, where Planck's constant commutes with position but not with momentum. Numerical computations of single-particle energies reveal significant shifts in deformations as the minimal length varies.

This paper introduces a novel random construction for generating polyphase complementary distributions in multi-dimensional arrays, which we term "weakly random PCW arrays." Detecting changes in hyperspectral images (HSI) presents a formidable challenge due to their extensive dimensionality, making the development of specialized algorithms for this task a difficult endeavor. This paper introduces a novel unsupervised approach that leverages deep learning to automatically extract deep features for subsequent change detection. Unlike many existing deep learning-driven methods that require pixel-level annotated changes for supervised training, this proposed framework is fully unsupervised, eliminating the dependency on labeled data. The algorithm utilizes a deep convolutional neuromodulator (DCNMM) to capture deep representations within a given HSI and employs feature fusion techniques to combine spectral data from multiple temporal visits, enhancing robustness. These fused spectral features are then compared against those from the other image to identify regions of difference. The effectiveness of this method is validated using two benchmark HSI datasets, demonstrating its practical application. Furthermore, the study provides a comprehensive analysis of various feature fusion strategies and evaluates the impact of different spectral stacking orders on overall performance.

We examine a linearly expanding cyclic cosmology inspired by $\Lambda$CDM theory, in which cycles alternate between an expansion phase and a contraction phase. In this model, cycles terminate via a "Big Rip," while $\Lambda$CDM theory is modified to remain consistent with the Big Rip concept. We demonstrate that this cyclic framework can be reconciled with current astronomical data by employing a specific parameterization that aligns the Big Rip event with a phase transition. This approach is implemented by substituting the cosmological constant with an effective dark energy potential. Furthermore, we establish that this cyclic cyclical structure can be described within the framework of modified $f(R)$ gravity.

Superdeterministic Bell-type quantum correlation models, such as the Invariant-set theory, are often criticized for lacking rigorous mathematical proof, appearing instead as ad-hic constructions. This paper examines whether Invariant-set theory functions as a specific, mathematically expressible hidden-variable model by attempting to generate its predictions through a well-defined physical framework. By exploring the Invariant-set theory using a general class of dynamical models for a variable, denoted as $\lambda(t)$, we assess the feasibility of deriving its outcomes. The analysis reveals that while this approach successfully predicts the Invariant-set theory's behavior for entanglement-based experiments, formulating a similar dynamical model that yields the correct Bell correlation statistics proves impossible. Consequently, we conclude that the Invariant-set theory cannot be realized as a simple time-evolution model for a single variable. To achieve the desired Bell correlations, any dynamical model must deviate from this formulation, requiring at least an additional degree of freedom.

Keyphrase spotting involves categorizing relevant phrases from user descriptions and is currently a standard NLP challenge. Traditionally, top-performing models rely on resource-intensive resources like GPUs, which are often unavailable for resource-constrained IoT devices; these machines typically can only rely on limited CPU power. To address this, we introduce a methodology that deploys state-of-the-art Transformer networks on IoT hardware. To mitigate these risks, it is essential to implement robust security and privacy measures, particularly for encryption. However, traditional encryption algorithms are often too computationally intensive for IoT devices, which lack the necessary processing power. This paper proposes a new approach to encryption specifically optimized for IoT devices with limited computational resources. The primary objective is to reduce both power consumption and encryption time. The core of this method involves a lightweight technique based on S-box generation using the Fibonacci sequence, which is then integrated with a variant of the AES algorithm. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm achieves significantly shorter key generation times ranging from 0.002 to 0.005 seconds, along with substantial power savings of 20% to 40% compared to existing methods.

This study examines the optimal experimental design for adaptive Ramsey sequences. A multi-qubit Ramsey measurement estimates a phase parameter $\phi$ by measuring the $Z$-component of each qubit's spin. By allowing for real-time updates of the posterior distribution of $\phi$ based on prior experimental results, the protocol becomes adaptive. We determine the optimal strategy for updating these qubit states between measurements, demonstrating that the conditional posterior distribution always remains factorizable. Furthermore, we derive analytic formulas for the variance of a maximum-likelihood estimator under this optimal strategy. The experimental variance is expressed as the inverse of the sum of classical and quantum Fisher Information. Finally, we validate the theoretical predictions through numerical simulations.

This work introduces a new gravitation model derived from a novel extension of General Relativity, characterized by azimuthal symmetry. A distinctive feature of the model is its reliance on two variables to define spacetime metrics: Cartesian coordinates and an auxiliary dimensionless variable, $\lambda$, which embodies azimuthal symmetry. Although $\lambda$ does not correspond to a physical dimension, it is symmetric with respect to rotation. The model's simplicity arises from the reduction of the Einstein-Hilbert action by one degree of freedom due to this symmetry, resulting in a modified Einstein equation that accounts for a correction term. By applying this formulation to a azimuthally symmetric Schwarzschild-de Witter black hole solution, the model predicts a specific event horizon radius given by $r_+=2M(1+\lambda_0)$, where $\lambda_0$ represents the initial value of $\lambda$. Furthermore, the model alters the Newtonian potential, introducing a $1/r^3$ component that causes a deviation from Newtonian gravity at small distances.

This work investigates properties of $n$-tuples of linear operators acting on a vector space and matrix bundles with linear operations defined on it. A primary objective is to delineate the structure of matrix operator bundles up to strict equivalence, establishing that they decompose into a direct sum comprising one instance each from the family $\mathbf{U}_\alpha$ and family $\mathbf{T}_\alpha$, where $\alpha$ ranges over $\mathbb{R}$ from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$. Furthermore, we introduce two distinct classes of linear operators on a vector space, denoted $\mathcal{U}$ and $\mathcal{T}$, and demonstrate that every bundle element at the strict type $\alpha$ is either from class $\mathcal{U}$ or class $\mathbf{T}$, but not both.

In recent years, representations of graphs using bounded treewidth have been employed to address various algorithmic challenges, particularly those related to graph minor complexity. This work introduces a new method for representing unweighted undirected planar graphs with a linear bound on their excluded minor depth (EMD). Specifically, if $n$ and $k$ are the graph's size and an integer representing an excluded minor depth, the graph is mapped to a tree of size $O(nk^2)$, where each edge is assigned a value not exceeding $k$. We term these *weighted tree representations* low-treewidth decompositions. This paper presents the first construction algorithm capable of building such representations in $O(nk^2 \log n)$ time. Moreover, we extend these concepts to weighted graphs, defining a metric low-treewidth representation that preserves distances within a multiplicative factor of $(1+\epsilon)$ and detail the corresponding linear-time construction algorithm.

This work investigates the long-term dynamics of smooth monotonicty-based discrete-time systems ($x_{t+1} = F(x_t)$) featuring compact convex domains, utilizing the theory of elliptic operators. A key innovation is the proof establishing that for strictly monotonic $F$, the system admits a unique positive-stable steady state located at the boundary, accompanied by an infinite spectrum of eigenfunctions where the leading two exhibit positive regions. Leveraging these findings, we demonstrate that for such systems, the measure of initial conditions leading to long-term convergence toward the unique stable equilibrium is full with respect to the measure $d\mu(x)$—a finding that extends the concept of prevalence in finite dimensions to infinite-dimensional spaces. Furthermore, we establish that the time average of functionals along trajectories originating from a fixed initial state $x_0$ almost surely equals the global time average computed over the entire state space with respect to $\mu$. These results generalize the Blueas-Yorke theorems, which address ordinary differential equations, to the specific domain of monotone, strongly monotone, and non-strictly monotonic systems.

Variational Quantum Eigensolvers (VQE) are widely recognized as a promising approach for approximating the ground state of quantum systems. However, their utility is often constrained by the extensive circuit depths required for traditional variational ansätze. This work introduces VQE-based algorithms that leverage single-qubit excitations, demonstrating that their success is highly dependent on the excitation amplitudes of the resulting ansatz state. Leveraging this insight, we developed a novel method that adaptively generates excitation-driven variational quantum ansätze with significantly lower circuit depths. Representations are typically learned by minimizing the representation's reconstruction error alongside a regularization term. In this work, we introduce a new approach to learn such representations by training a latent variable model—specifically, a probabilistic model capable of representing the underlying data distribution—with the goal of maximizing its likelihood given the data. Although this concept is conceptually straightforward, we demonstrate that applying variational inference to map maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimates of latent variables effectively yields superior representations for a variety of tasks. Our findings indicate that the proposed method is particularly advantageous when the available data is limited. Furthermore, we show that the optimal architecture for the latent variable model is a hierarchical one, where higher-level latent variables condition lower-level ones in a cascade.

The recent NANOGrav 11-year dataset, which reveals a common-spectrum process (CSP) in the gravitational-wave (GW) background, offers a unique opportunity to constrain the physics of inflation. The stiff-fluid amplification model, a scenario where inflationary energy rapidly reionizes into a GW background that remains unchanged by the subsequent equation of state evolution, is examined here. This model predicts a nearly scale-invariant spectrum extending from nano-Hertz frequencies up to those detected by Advanced LIGO and Virgo. Specifically, the amplified background would dominate the nano-Hertz CSP signal by a factor exceeding $10^3$ and would generate a GW merger rate surpassing $10^{-2}$ per cubic megaparsec per year within the Advanced LIGO and Virgo sensitivity window. These high-frequency merger rates would directly contradict current observations, thereby ruling out this specific stiff-fluid inflationary model. Furthermore, such a background would significantly enhance the GW standard siren measurement of the Hubble constant ($H_0$) to $10\%$ precision, potentially alleviating the existing tension with cosmological estimates derived from the CMB.

We report the inaugural observations of a comet using the ALMA Atacama Compact Array (ACA), a system comprising eight antennas. Utilizing the ACA's extensive field of view, we conducted a survey of the system's extended emission, specifically targeting carbon monosulfide ($CS$) around C/2015 ER61 (PanSTARRS) during its perihelion passage. Data were gathered via broad-bandwidth ($\sim 100$ MHz) observations at 43.3 GHz ($\sim 6.9$ cm wavelength), which revealed emission extending up to 0.05 au from the nucleus. Analysis of broad-band images yielded a flux density of $0.29 \pm 0.01$ Jy at 43.3 GHz, corresponding to an emission measure of $1.1 \pm 0.1 \times 10^{15}$ molecules cm$^{-2}$. This emission measure is notably higher than values derived from $CO^+$ observations of the same object, which instead yielded $2.1 \times 10^{14}$ molecules cm$^{-2}$. Such a disparity suggests a dispersed source for $CS$ that exceeds $CO^+$ release, potentially due to the radiative dissociation of $CS_2$ in the coma.

Unsupervised speech synthesis (USP) enables speech generation for spoken words without requiring labeled datasets. While recent advances in deep learning have significantly improved USP performance, these methods typically rely on intricate architectures and demanding pre-training procedures. This paper introduces a novel, uncomplicated, and highly effective USP framework that utilizes speech-enhancement and speaker-encoding models to achieve superior results compared to existing methods. Specifically, our system employs an end-to-end approach using a simple Transformer for speech enhancement and incorporates a speaker-encoder trained on separate out-of-domain data. Additionally, our text-to-music encoder employs connected components to handle unknown words efficiently. Extensive experiments on the LibriSpeech dataset confirm the efficacy of this method, demonstrating that it surpasses current state-of-the-art performance in terms of both simplicity and efficacy.

This study investigates a complex-based Holographic Dark Energy (HDE) model, referred to as the Essence model, which extends the standard framework by incorporating a complex-valued canonical density. The viability of this construction is confirmed as the derived energy density remains positive. Furthermore, the model's dynamics are analyzed using a Tsallis non-extensive framework to determine the associated equation of state. By integrating these dynamics within the context of the $\Lambda$CDM framework, the study explores the model's cosmological behavior, specifically focusing on the late-time evolution of HDE. The findings indicate that the complex form of HDE successfully replicates the observed cosmological data, including the transition from a matter-dominated phase to an $\Lambda$CDM-like state.

Multi-Objective Mixed-Integer Non-Linear Programming (MO-MINLP) problems are prevalent across diverse fields, such as energy, finance, and engineering. Although established algorithms exist for similar problems, they often fail to address the specific challenges inherent to large-scale MO-MINLPs. This study introduces a novel approach, denoted as NSGAII-Branch and Bound (NSGAII-BnB), which leverages the well-known Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGAII). The proposed method treats each branch in the BnB framework as a subproblem and applies the NSGAII algorithm to them. The effectiveness of NSGAII-BnB was validated through extensive testing on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Results indicate that the approach delivers high-quality solutions that surpass the performance of the underlying "parent" NSGAII algorithm. Furthermore, when compared to the state-of-the-art method by Adjodoh et al. (2019), the NSGAII-BnB approach yields solutions of superior quality.

In a setting where the classical real numbers $\mathbb{R}$ are replaced by a ring of dual numbers, we demonstrate that every connected Lie groupoid acts on any subsheft containing nilpotent elements exactly as a nilpotent vector field does on a smooth manifold, with these actions being identical on the level of classical geometry. This generalization extends the previous finding regarding Lie group consistency by incorporating groupoids, thereby supporting applications in the local theory involving groupoid integrations such as within topos-based differential geometry.

The accelerating pace of biomedical research is driven by a need for larger datasets and complex, x86-based analytical workflows that span these data sources. However, current data access mechanisms are often rigid and fail to accommodate the diverse, dynamic, and evolving nature of biomedical computing environments. To address this, we introduce a flexible framework for sharing biomedical research data and analysis code through "cyberinfrastructure gateways." This approach enables users to execute code on extensive computing resources without requiring direct data transfer, while also providing developers with a standardized interface for varied cyberinfrastructures. We have implemented such gateways for three major repositories—NCI Genomic Epidemiology Program, the Cancer Genome Atlas, and the Encyclopedia of DNA Elements—demonstrating that these solutions offer more effective access pathways compared to traditional methods.

Aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) aims to determine the sentiment polarity of specific components within texts. While recent advances in deep learning have significantly improved ABSP performance, they often fail to capture the nuanced, multi-dimensional emotional context of these aspects. To address this, we introduce a new framework that employs a new approach to effectively model implicit sentiment. We develop the model by integrating two innovative techniques: (1) the application of Supervised Contrastive Pre-training (SCPP) to enhance emotional representations, and (2) the implementation of an emotion-aware self-attention mechanism to enrich the interaction between aspects and sentences. Our extensive evaluations on three public benchmarks, including ABS-IAI and SemEval-14, demonstrate that the proposed model significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art results.

We develop methods for estimating indices related to indirect effects and total effects in causal processes involving an intervening binary variable, specifically utilizing the Case-Control Linear-Probit (CLP) framework which combines linear treatments and outcomes with logistic mediation. This approach samples treated individuals and controls, allowing for the exploration of effect decomposition through mediation analysis. Effect identification within CLP models requires either knowledge of the sampling design or the use of inverse probability weighting. Additionally, we propose a flexible estimation technique based on weighted maximum likelihood estimation with augmented CLP samples that does not necessitate balancing the sampled dataset; instead, it estimates parameters using the full population while accounting for sampling weights. Simulation results indicate that the weighted maximum likelihood estimator performs robustly across diverse scenarios, remaining reliable even when applied to subsamples. Furthermore, the method demonstrates significant efficiency gains compared to analyses that fail to incorporate weighting information. Applied to data from the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1979, we find that linear-probit mediation with sampled mediators yields estimates consistent with those derived from unadjusted samples.

This study investigates secure multi-user communication networks enhanced by Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS), accounting for hardware impairments. We propose a joint design strategy to achieve secure optimal robust transmit vectors that minimize the aggregate mean square error under these impairments. To address the resulting non-convex constraints, we apply the Successive Convex Approximation (SCA) method, transforming the problem into a sequence of convex sub-problems that can be solved iteratively. To further enhance robustness and reliability, we incorporate a worst-case analysis to ensure robust optimal transmission vectors. Finally, we present a set of simulation results demonstrating the performance of the proposed scheme.

The Parker Solar Probe (PSP) mission is designed to measure solar wind conditions within the corona, beginning with a perihelion passage of 8.86 solar radii. This study presents the initial findings from energy flux spectra of electron, ion, and neutral species recorded by these instruments. The spectral energy flux follows a power-law distribution with slopes of approximately -2 for electrons and ions, and -5/3 for neutral atoms. These slopes are consistent with a turbulent cascade of kinetic energy and the "Solar Wind Breeze" model, respectively, across the entire dataset. Furthermore, energy flux calculations for species like protons and neutral atoms reveal a radial gradient in flux that aligns with Goldstein et al.'s (2007) solar wind breeze model, which attributes this effect primarily to radial turbulence. The data also indicate that spectral breaks in electron energy distribution occur at significantly lower energies than those seen in ion distributions. Additionally, enhanced spectral breaks in proton distributions are observed during high plasma beta events, and spectral breaks in neutral atom distributions are more pronounced at high temperatures.

We present a noncommutative generalization of the concept of a principal bundle over a countable open covering, derived directly from the action of the bundle's structure group on its associated $C^*$-algebra. This framework establishes the relationship between such bundles and their total spaces through their free action on $C^*$-algebras. The resulting classification of these noncommutative principal bundles is achieved by examining the universal principal bundle, which is shown to be universal specifically within the context of free actions exerted by certain noncommuting principal type groups on $C^*$-algebras. The proof utilizes the equivalence relation framework alongside functorial methods to achieve these results.

This study investigates how $q$-deformation affects both the clarity and the acceleration (or deceleration, i.e., slow/fast light) of light propagation within the context of an optomechanical system featuring two atomic ensembles. The configuration consists of an optical cavity coupled to two distinct cavities, each interacting with its own optomechanical cell, where the cavity modes are driven by an external drive field and damped by a corresponding mirror. The analysis indicates that $q$-deformation plays a significant role in regulating light clarity and controlling the velocity of transmitted light.

We introduce a neural network approach for solving hyperbolic and parabolic types partial differential equations. The method is built upon a cell-centered finite volume scheme utilizing linear reconstruction at cell boundaries. The solution is derived by satisfying integral forms of these equations directly at discrete cells, with the weakly imposed boundary and initial conditions applied on this neural network solution. The research demonstrates that this cell-centrist based finite volume approach is effective for solving a broad range of equations, including those involving nonlinear source terms, mixed elliptic-parabolic characteristics, and complex physical setups.

The ALICE experiment is designed to investigate the characteristics of the hot, dense, and short-lived nuclear matter created during heavy-ion collisions at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). While the facility recently concluded its data collection for LHC Run 3, ALICE has already initiated its first extra experiments beyond the LHC's primary running cycles. This article examines enhancements planned for ALICE to operate beyond Run 3, detailing the scientific objectives that will drive these upgrades, the specific technical enhancements required, and the associated technological innovations, with a focus on the upgrade of the central tracking system, the addition of new detectors, and improvements to the electromagnetic spectrometer and the internal tracking system.

We introduce a theoretical framework for simulating the timelike Unruh effect, involving an observer who traverses inside their own future and past light cones. By analyzing an experimental setup featuring an object moving along a circular trajectory within an artificial, timelike region, we demonstrate that its quantum phase accumulation exhibits a specific geometric component known as the Berry phase. We provide a detailed calculation for both the curvature associated with this timelike domain and the resulting Berry phase. Furthermore, we illustrate that these effects, which depend on the observer's velocity, serve as indicators for the timelike version of the Unruh phenomenon. Unsurprisingly, both the magnitude of these phases scales linearly with acceleration; this acceleration acts as the crucial parameter governing the influence and enables the practical observation of the effect.

Disaster incidents are frequently documented in diverse formats, including informal social media posts and official documents, often featuring multilingual content and unstructured data. Traditional disaster-incident extraction methods, built on structured news reports, frequently prove inadequate for multilingual social media content. To address this gap, we introduce the Multilingual Incident Extraction (MEE) dataset, comprising over 10,000 annotations across 11 languages for identifying and categorizing incidents. We further evaluate a novel model based on a transformer architecture, utilizing query and context embedding strategies alongside label embedding techniques. Our findings reveal that incorporating these strategies substantially enhances annotation consistency and performance.

For instance $G$ as the algebraic Grassmannian, where the Grassmannian of $k$-planes in $n$-space is denoted by $G=G(k,n)$, and $c_i(G)$ represents the coefficients in the total Chern class $c(T) = \sum c_i(T)$ of a complex vector bundle $T$, this paper investigates the integral of a polynomial constructed from these Chern numbers over a closed, smooth, and compact complex manifold $X$. The focus involves the integral over $X$ of the term $p_*(c_m(G))$, where $p_*$ is the push-forward operation for a specific rank-$k$ vector bundle $T$ on $X$. The analysis covers the general properties of this operation and demonstrates that the resulting cohomology components $p_*(c_i(T))$ are positive whenever the degree $m$ is sufficiently large. The discussion also addresses applications regarding the zero sets of generic sections and provides further examples illustrating these findings.

This study investigates the stellar breeze from the companion star in the high-mass black hole binary system Cyg X-1, specifically examining its impact on X-ray spectra and timing data during the hard state. The analysis reveals that the stellar breeze accounts for approximately 10% of the source's X-ray flux. The observed spectral and temporal variations correlate directly with the companion's orbital phase, confirming their origin in the breeze. We detect a distinct high-energy cutoff at approximately 100 keV, which fluctuates between 50 and 150 keV depending on the orbital phase. Furthermore, the magnitude of the Comptonization parameter ($y$) aligns with expectations for the Comptonization of X-rays escaping the stellar atmosphere. Our findings indicate that the Comptonization parameter varies by a factor of two across different orbital phases, driven by changes in the electron temperature and density within the companion star. The specific mechanisms governing these fluctuations in electron and proton densities remain unclear. Additionally, we identify a correlation between the Comptonization parameter and the power ratio of high-frequency (100–300 Hz) to low-frequency (10–50 Hz) variability, a relationship likely mediated by the density of the stellar breeze.

This work examines a vector field non-chiral EFT featuring a non-abelian ether-like interaction. While a naive construction of the ether term is not gauge-invariant, a specific modification achieves this property, mirroring the structure of the Standard Model Extension. Key dynamics include the possibility of extra terms, the emergence of both light and heavy modes, and the resulting behavior of these modes at various temperatures. Analysis of the high-temperature regime reveals that the light modes are governed by an entropy function derived from the original ether-like term, whereas the high-energy contributions from heavy modes scale linearly with temperature. These findings are then applied to a scenario extending the electroweak sector with a vector field, specifically examining the implications for a polarized photon gas.

We propose a new approach to parsing that performs syntax and semantic parsing simultaneously. Instead of treating semantics as arguments attached to the argument structure, we implement it as modifications to the standard context-free grammar rules. This is achieved by enriching the production rules with the arguments required by each non-terminal, effectively integrating semantic requirements directly into the syntactic form. By merging the syntactic and semantic state spaces into a unified state, we can leverage the strengths of both representations within a single decoding process. Evaluating our approach across multiple languages, including English and multilingual scenarios, demonstrates that this joint strategy yields significant improvements in parsing accuracy. Specifically, the technique enhances the precision of semantic parsing by approximately 10% and the accuracy of syntactic parsing by about 3%, relative to previous best-in-class results.

We examine magnetized, neutrino-cooled disks that form following the merger of compact objects, specifically investigating how jet outflows evolve from the disk. Our methodology involves adapting a previously developed general-relativistic, radiation-magnetized, hydrodynamical code to simulate JET shocks emerging from the context of Neutrino-cooled Accretion Disks (JADs). Our findings indicate that jets launched from such disks exhibit dynamics comparable to those seen in black hole binary mergers, driven by magnetic energy extraction from the rotating, magnetized material rather than disk reprocessing alone. Our simulations reveal jet speeds reaching approximately 0.8 times the speed of light ($0.8c$), with isotropic equivalent energies around $10^{51}$ erg. Furthermore, we analyze the jet's interaction with the surrounding radiation field, offering a specific focus on the mechanisms by which JADs contribute to JET shocks.

Using 320 HSC-SSP137 images, we have identified a sample of 1,000 early-type galaxies (ETGs) with redshifts between 0.05 and 0.25, utilizing a magnitude range of $18 < \text{m}_{\text{r}} < 24$. By examining the flux distribution of tidal structures, we found that approximately 10% of these galaxies possess significant tidal features, defined as $f_t > 0.01$. The likelihood of possessing such features increases with magnitude and declines as redshift rises. Assuming tidal features are the remnants of major mergers, we calculated an average merger rate of roughly 0.02 per ETG, which is roughly double the rate observed for spiral galaxies. Furthermore, we determined that nearly 20% of galaxies in our magnitude-limited sample have undergone a significant merger within the last 1 Gyr, a proportion that grows to over 40% among the brightest galaxies. These findings indicate that ETGs in the local universe are currently experiencing a more intense recent history of major mergers than previously understood, a trend that likely extends to lower redshift levels.

In the first article of this series, I introduced the Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation (ASTG), which posits that gravitating masses generate a specific, novel gravitational field. Building on this foundation, subsequent theories have explored the complex field created by two such masses. The present study, the second in the series, examines the interaction between two masses and reveals that the resulting field not only drives the masses toward each other but also creates a distinct region along the symmetry axis where the field acts repulsively. The present paper focuses on analyzing the repellent behavior observed specifically on this axis.

Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are brief, intense millisecond-long signals detected in the radio spectrum. While their origins remain uncertain, leading theories suggest a connection to neutron stars, though the lack of multi-wavelength follow-up observations has prevented their discovery. This study reports the analysis of 1,133 FRBs from the CHIME/FRB database, examining high-cadence optical data from the OGLE survey and CHIME/FPSM. No fast radio emission was found in 103 FRBs with confirmed high-confidence counterparts in the optical domain. Furthermore, searches for delayed or simultaneous optical flashes yielded null results for 103 cases and 10 additional cases, respectively. These findings place stringent upper limits on the energy of fast optical radiation, specifically $E_{\rm opt} < 10^{39}$ erg for optical flashes and $E_{\rm opt} < 10^{40}$ erg for fast optical flashes. Consequently, these limits on fast optical radiation are comparable to existing constraints from radio searches, offering valuable insights for models regarding neutron star origins of FRBs.

This work details the modeling, analysis, and redesign of two high-power laser systems: a 100-W edge-emitting diode laser and a 100-W slab laser amplifier. In redesigning these devices, the goal was to elevate their output power while simultaneously improving thermal performance through reduced temperature gradients and more uniform power distribution. We examined the thermophysical behavior of the original devices to validate our findings using finite element simulations. Furthermore, we applied reverse engineering to a novel edge-emitting diode laser system to evaluate its performance.

It is widely recognized that large language models (LLMs) can be instructed to perform visual tasks such as image captioning and visual question answering through instruction tuning. In contrast, this study demonstrates an alternative approach where we achieve the same by integrating visual capabilities directly into the text generation process. Our proposed method involves incorporating external visual predictors as conditional modules within the decoder of an LLM. During generation, these visual components function as specialized agents that allow the model to perceive images while producing text. We introduce a straightforward architecture for the decoder that enables the joint optimization of the model's generation and perception components. Experiments show that this approach not only allows for end-to-end image captioning but also transfers effectively to tasks like visual captioning.

We introduce a modified RingCT variant that shrinks the digital signature on every single input within a transaction while keeping the signature size around the input count unchanged but making it significantly smaller and simpler than in the original version optimized for faster verification tools used by miners. This improvement speeds up verification times for the entire transaction set without compromising privacy or security, allowing for faster block processing by miners. By leveraging a new small-size signature scheme we show that verification latency can be greatly reduced so transaction validation becomes more efficient even when handling transaction sets containing numerous inputs. We introduce a collaborative framework for constructing data-driven reduced-order models, leveraging the strengths of both distributed and global data. This approach addresses both the global model reduction task and the critical challenge of identifying the optimal data blend for task-specific training. We demonstrate that by integrating ideas from multi-agent collaboration, index-based data compression, and global model updating, the method can not only produce highly accurate global models but also facilitate the efficient, parallel processing of data across nodes. Specifically, we utilize the proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) to extract compressed data indices and then employ a data compression technique to merge these indices into an enhanced global model. We test this framework on a network of agents, each managing a data partition from a fluid dynamics simulation of flow past a cylinder. The results indicate that our strategy yields performance superior to traditional methods, which rely solely on either data partitioning or the entire dataset.

This study examines $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(nS)\pi^+\pi^-$ decays via $\Upsilon(nS)\pi^+\pi^-$ final states (where $n=1,2,3,4,5$) using the hadronic loop mechanism. We calculate the partial decay widths for the $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(nS)\pi^+\pi^-$ processes and assess the experimental branching fractions expected from Belle II. Additionally, we determine the relative contributions of the $\Upsilon(10860)$ and $\Upsilon(10856)$ states to the $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(nS)\pi^+\pi^-$ decay channels. Our results indicate that the $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(nS)\pi^+\pi^-$ branching ratios are non-negligible for $n=1,2,3,4,5$, while the hadronic loop mechanism is applicable. We also evaluate the feasibility of the $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(nS)\pi^+\pi^-$ decay channel for Belle II experiments.

Training neural networks to run on edge devices often necessitates quantizing weights and activations, yet the vast search space of potential quantization configurations typically hinders finding optimal solutions. This paper introduces a novel training methodology that integrates the annealing strategy of Single Stochastic Gradient Descent with constraints that keep quantized weights within a specific interval. The approach employs a dual-quantization configuration: weights utilize a step function with an offset, while the objective function incorporates both L2 regularization relative to the ideal floating-point parameters and a constraint based on the theoretical gradient magnitude. These specific conditions ensure the objective function remains a convex optimization problem solvable via closed-form equations. Empirical results demonstrate that Single Stochastic Gradient Descent with quantized weights and a double-quantization objective is highly effective for quantized neural network optimization. Furthermore, the study examines the impact of varying the number of intervals and annealing schedules on both optimal solution discovery and convergence velocity. Finally, it evaluates a proposed extension where weights utilize a step function without offset against standard single-SGDD algorithms, confirming that this new method is highly effective.

Soft robotics represents a rapidly expanding field with growing potential for real-world applications, though its complex, nonlinear dynamics have long hindered effective control. Addressing these difficulties, researchers have introduced various mathematical models, which, though diverse in approach, have significantly advanced the field. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of existing soft robot modeling techniques and evaluates how each specifically impacts control performance. Furthermore, we analyze outstanding challenges and emerging research directions aimed at enhancing model-driven control methods.

This work demonstrates that the genuine Jacobi group is isomorphic to the semi-direct product of $SL_2(\mathbb{R})$ and the semi-direct product formed by $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$. We also demonstrate that this decomposition holds isomorphically for the non-genuine $n$-fold cover of the group. These isomorphisms yield convenient semi-direct product representations of metaplectic type groups associated with the true Jacobi group.

This study addresses the challenge of table-based fact verification, a difficult task requiring models to navigate complex issues like missing data, informal structures, and cards embedded within text or tables. We introduce a strategy for dissecting, or decomposing, these mixed-form tables to isolate individual components, such as missing cells and individual cards, converting them into linear structures. This transforms subsequent fact-checking into a multi-stage process involving both structural analysis and logical reasoning. Our approach demonstrates that decomposition is effective, achieving state-of-the-art results on the CheckTable dataset.

Although generative adversarial networks (GANs) are highly effective for generating realistic images, they typically lack interpretability regarding the parameters governing their learned data distributions. In response, researchers have developed techniques to impose conditioning constraints on GANs, notably through image and text inputs. However, these approaches often result in GANs that are difficult to control. In contrast, our study introduces a novel approach utilizing an intrinsic latent variable to establish a concealed conditioning framework within GANs. By disentangling the latent representation into generative and conditional components, our precludes unwanted interaction between these factors, thereby granting the model heightened controllability. The technique effectively separates the latent code into independent parts, enhancing controllability. Empirical evaluations on the CelebA and LSUN Cat-Dog datasets confirm that our approach not only produces high-quality images but also enables the isolation of individual attributes and the execution of fine-grained control.

Nested sampling is a Bayesian technique for inferring model parameters and comparing competing models. Its execution relies on two core components: a likelihood calculator and a selector for nested hyperparameters. This research focuses on optimizing the selector, with potential improvements offering significant gains in efficiency for complex model applications. By benchmarking four different strategies against both synthetic data and real observational records, we determine that the most efficient approach is one that selects the fixed top fraction of samples for every iteration. Conversely, early stage iterations should retain a broader set of accepted proposals to ensure robustness.

The distance labeling problem seeks to assign labels to vertices such that a vertex $u$ can reach distance $k$ from vertex $v$ if and only if $u$ can read $v$ at that distance. This sequence of labels is denoted as distance-$k$ labeling. While an optimal solution would use labels of length 1, achieving this remains an unsolved challenge even for trees. However, efficient algorithms exist that produce optimal distance labelings for specific graph families, particularly planar ones. This study presents the first constant-factor approximation algorithm for computing the minimum length of distance labels in planar graphs that remain resilient to single faults. A distance label is considered fault-resilient if the distance between any two non-adjacent vertices changes by at most 1 following the removal of a single vertex. Our approach leverages a fault-resilient distance labeling of tree-based structures, specifically utilizing the result from B\"{u}chler et al. (2019) which provides a fault-tolerant hierarchy of labels with a fault tolerance of 1 for distance labels in trees of size $O(\log n)$. This method is extended to construct a fault-tolerant hierarchy of labels with a fault tolerance of 1 for distance labels in planar graphs of size $O(n)$. Our main contribution is a fault-tolerant hierarchy of labels with a fault tolerance of 1 for distance labels in planar graphs of size $O(n)$.

We introduce a computationally efficient method for calculating in-time and in-frequency two-particle correlation functions within the numerically tractable Gaussian approximation. These additional channels for analyzing correlations complement the standard real-time and real-space perspectives. Using a Hamiltonian under Gaussian approximation, we demonstrate the application of these metrics to a driven-dissipative Bose-Hubbbar model, specifically examining the influence of nonlinear dissipation on both interference contrast and peak separation in time and frequency. We find that in-time spatial separation acts as a discriminator: while single-particle distributions remain constant for both hard-core and soft-core interactions, the two-particle temporal correlations differ, allowing us to distinguish between distinct interaction regimes. We also derive the steady-state two-particle frequency spectrum, demonstrating that even in the mean-field limit, frequency-domain correlations remain sensitive to the nature of the particles.

Recent studies have demonstrated value in leveraging statistical strata for identifying out-of-distribution samples, though they rely on fixed distributions that fail to account for shifts in data due to distributional drift. To address this limitation, we introduce a data-driven method for learning latent Gaussian Gaussian strata, enabling more precise identification of distributional drift and subsequent detection of samples that fall outside this distribution. We empirically validate the approach on synthetic scenarios and practical applications involving phase information and strata modeling.

We investigate a two-dimensional two-species model of particles in an undamped, open system with optical lattices, where the particles are subject to Floquet engineering. Under these conditions, the system stabilizes a unique state characterized by infinite entanglement and order similar to a scar state, which defies the predictions of equilibrium statistical mechanics. Specifically, the particles display second-order spatial coherence and condensation within a quasi-momentum space at the lattice center, occupying just the lowest Floquet band. In contrast, particle number fluctuations remain negligible, and the distribution of higher Floquet bands is minimal. These characteristics resemble those of an isolated many-body scar state. However, unlike isolated scars, this state exists within an open system and results from quantum interference between driving-induced tunneling and dissipation, occurring despite the lack of an exact mirror-symmetry in the quantum jump operators. The study further demonstrates that this state is robust against variations in the driving scheme and experimental parameters, suggesting a viable potential for achieving unique non-equilibrium order in experimentally accessible open systems.

In this paper, we establish an improved Alexandrov maximum principle and uniform Hölder continuity for solutions of the Monge–Ampère equation. These findings enhance and generalize the relevant work found in the research by Kim and in the research by Figalli, Figalli, and Savin.

Optical clocks represent the pinnacle of timekeeping accuracy. While current research focuses on developing devices with extended operation periods, the inherent noise in the light used for reading these clocks poses a significant challenge. This paper proposes a novel statistical framework for time-domain analysis of non-periodic time series data derived from optical clock operations. By applying this method to both the clock output and the environmental inputs, we identify specific mechanisms by which environmental fluctuations impact the clock's performance. Ultimately, this approach provides a vital foundation for refining control strategies in next-generation, high-accuracy optical timing systems.

This study introduces a real-time Software-Defined Networking (SDN) architecture enhanced with fog computing to manage Service Function Chaining (SFC) service function proxies (SFPs) across distributed data centers. Our approach utilizes machine learning to forecast future SFP demands, enabling the system to optimize resource allocation within edge servers and facilitate SFP migration between them. Specifically, we employ an artificial neural network (ANN) to predict future network traffic patterns, which drives the use of the Tabu Search algorithm for selecting optimal SFP placement and resource allocation strategies. These strategies are designed to minimize energy consumption, reduce latency, and prevent system faults. Simulation results demonstrate that our proposed architecture significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art solutions in terms of SFP placement efficiency, resource utilization, fault mitigation, and overall energy savings.

Gradient surgery serves as an analytical tool for examining optimization dynamics, while the selection of an appropriate loss function is pivotal for achieving desired model performance. This study investigates the interaction between these factors by applying gradient surgery to a simple predictive coding scenario. We evaluated multiple common loss functions and discovered that standard analyses using gradient surgery can be misleading when specific losses are employed, necessitating the use of our proposed "shooting" gradient surgery variant. This adapted method reveals crucial insights, including an understanding of how loss functions influence curvature and their intrinsic relationship to Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence.

We introduce the hyper-invariant MERA (HiMER A), a new family of quantum error-correcting (ECC) codes that expands upon holographic MERAs by incorporating hyperbolic invariant manifolds (HiMMs). These codes feature significant power-law dependencies between the bulk and boundary, enabling efficient identification of code words and simulation of quantum dynamics via the hyperbolic renormalization group. Additionally, their unique structure facilitates an enhanced holographic ECC with stronger error-correction resilience compared to earlier implementations.

We analyzed the spacing distribution using a sliding window technique with a fixed width of 10 arcseconds. The analysis reveals that the most probable spacing distance is approximately 100 arcseconds. Additionally, we observed a significant increase in the likelihood of finding closer filaments as the distance decreases below 100 arcseconds, and a corresponding decrease in the likelihood of finding more distant ones beyond this scale. The nonstochastic bandit framework is currently being extended to scenarios where delays inherent to regret mechanisms influence the choice of subsequent actions. Previous investigations into delay-agnostic and parameterized delay models have established various outcomes, yet a model accounting for arm-specific (item-dependent) delays remains unexplored. This paper introduces a novel non-convex parameter estimation task that arises in this context. By developing a new algorithm and rigorously analyzing it, we demonstrate that achieving minimax optimal performance is possible for this problem under specific conditions. Conversely, we prove that reaching minimax optimality is impossible in other configurations. Additionally, we draw a direct connection between this bandit scenario and a novel advisor problem characterized by arm-dependent lags (time-lagged advice). Similar to the bandit setting, we derive both lower and upper bounds for the ideal performance of this advisor variant across diverse delay patterns.

Dialogue dialog systems are increasingly vital in various sectors, yet they often fail to mimic the natural conversational flow exhibited by humans. To address this limitation, we introduce LEATHER, a learning framework designed to generate human-like responses for open-domain, multi-turn dialogues. By utilizing a two-stage approach, LEATHER first collects high-quality human-computer interactions and subsequently trains a language model to synthesize a realistic distribution of these interactions. We developed two specific evaluation metrics to assess the human-likeness of synthetic texts: (1) a semantic similarity measure comparing synthetic outputs to real conversations, and (2) a blind comparison between human-written and system-produced texts. Our experimental findings indicate that our proposed approach not only outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods but also provides a robust framework for evaluating the authenticity of text within open-domain dialogue contexts.

The work presented examines $2+1$ flavor lattice QCD simulations across the range of baryon chemical potentials ($\mu_B$) from 0 to 0.8 fm$^{-1}$. These calculations, performed at temperatures ($T$) between 0.12 and 0.30 fm$^{-1}$, utilize gauge actions derived from the highly improved Schaefer action alongside improved lattice operators. The study focuses on mesonic and baryonic correlation functions, with an analysis of systematic errors arising from discretization and finite lattice spacing. Results are compared against continuum extrapolations and existing data from collaborations such as CLS, BMW, and QCDSFB. Additionally, we incorporate findings from a recent QCDSFB paper to extend the coverage of simulated densities.

This paper introduces a novel probabil surrogate model designed to simulate offshore wind turbine loads and the resulting structural stresses. By utilizing chained Gaussian processes (GP), the method links time-series data from key aerodynamic variables—specifically tower base bending moments, rotor thrust, and yaw moment—to standard strain time-series at the blade root. The approach evaluates stress time-series by projecting loads onto the first principal component of the strain distribution, which is modeled using a GP, and subsequently inferring uncertainties in this transformation. Validation against the OpenFAST simulator demonstrates that these surrogate predictions align closely with OpenFAST outcomes, achieving significantly lower computational costs.

Natural disasters can be anticipated, mitigated, and managed more effectively by analyzing social media, which offers a rapid, inexpensive, and comprehensive data source. This study examines Twitter activity concerning recent earthquakes in Izmir, Turkey, utilizing statistical methods to evaluate tweet volume, posting times, tweet density radii, and language distribution. The analysis of user language types and geospatial distribution of tweet ranges around the epicenter highlights the advantage of combining location-based data for monitoring disasters. Ultimately, this research aims to support decision-makers in improving decision-making processes related to disaster management.

A group $G$ exhibits the property $R_\infty$ relative to its word map if, for every quadratic nilpotent lower central series quotient of $G$, exactly half of the group's elements result in the identity. The authors demonstrate that this specific $R_\infty$ property holds for all such quotients derived from generalized abelian Baumslag-Solitar groups.

We present a trajectory-basis, forward-optimization approach for inversion, which is applied to time-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (TR-PE). This method solves an inverse problem by treating the initial state vector as unknown variables and directly optimizing them via algorithms like stochastic gradient descent (SGD), utilizing a time-dependent solution derived from a forward-evolving model. Demonstrated through a trajectory-basis expansion applied to TR-PE data involving a two-level system, our results show the technique recovers the initial state vector with high fidelity. Importantly, the method yields robust outcomes even when dealing with noisy experimental data or scenarios marked by high information content, where the potential for overfitting remains. Additionally, the computational cost is significantly reduced compared to standard iterative schemes, as the evolution step is executed only once per optimization iteration. Finally, recent advancements in traint-based models utilizing GPUs are highlighted, illustrating their capacity to handle large-scale inverse problems with remarkable efficiency.

Naturalistic Driving Data (NDD) serves as a valuable asset for developing and evaluating models in autonomous driving, offering driving scenarios that are more diverse than those found in standard test sets. Nevertheless, real-world driving scenarios are highly intricate, and current NDDs often lack sufficient detail to support rigorous driving scenario recognition. Consequently, this study introduces SceNDD, a comprehensive naturalistic driving dataset designed to facilitate driving scenario recognition. The dataset was gathered from 12 vehicles across 11 cities in China, featuring 1,000 hours of high-fidelity recordings from 2021. It incorporates multi-modal data—including camera feeds, high-resolution maps, and precise positioning and tracking data for the ego-vehicle and surrounding agents. Furthermore, we propose a novel framework for scenario recognition that leverages structural differences among scenarios. Experimental results indicate that utilizing this proposed method along with the provided annotations allows for significantly improved performance in driving scenario recognition.

Boundary and interface conformal models are characterized by a specific structure where the system decomposes into two subsystems, $A$ and $B$, linked by an interface separating boundary conformal theories within each subsystem. This study introduces a boundary conformal field model featuring such a boundary/interface structure and proposes a method to calculate the reflection entropy for the entire model, its $A$ and $B$ components, as well as their interfacial boundary regions. Additionally, analytical formulas for the reflection entropy of finite chains of $A$ and $B$ are derived, showing that the reflection entropy of the total boundary/interface configuration equals the sum of the reflections entropies of the individual boundary segments in each theory. These findings are validated through numerical computations of finite $A$ and $B$ systems and their associated interfaces. Finally, the behavior of reflection entropy in the thermodynamic limit for the full boundary/interface structure is analyzed, demonstrating that the model's entropy vanishes when the subsystem dimensions remain fixed while the total chain length approaches infinity.

Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS) have emerged as a promising technology for enhancing 5G and future networks by optimizing the wireless environment. In this context, the channel matrix serves as a critical factor, as it enables simultaneous transmission of high-dimensional data streams. However, acquiring full knowledge of these large-dimensional matrices is resource-intensive and unnecessary. This paper introduces a sparse channel estimation technique for RIS-assisted Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) that utilizes an Enhanced Extreme Learning Machine (ELM) trained on features extracted from pilot symbols. The proposed method operates effectively even when relying on shortened cyclic prefixes (missing orthogonal guarantees in compression) and accounting for practical hardware imperfections, such as phase errors and amplitude mismatches. These issues, which typically degrade RIS channel performance, are mitigated by the proposed machine learning approach. Simulation results demonstrate that the enhanced ELM-based estimator outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency.

Biological brains are considered the most sophisticated information processing systems currently known to humanity. Although quantum computing has made significant strides in recent years, the application of quantum information science to the study of neural systems remains largely unexplored. This review reviews the potential of quantum data for creating a new framework to analyze brain activity. The discussion centers on the neurophysics of consciousness, the neurobiology of memory, and the neuroscience of perception. These topics illustrate how incorporating quantum data could enhance the comprehension of brain function.

This work introduces a tool that generates an ACL2 logic certificate for a given C program, effectively producing a shalow embedding of that C code within ACL2. The resulting certificate, when combined with the ACL2 CNF checker, can verify properties of C programs. Additionally, by repurposing this certificate, the tool serves to synthesize both a counterexample in the original C code and a complete proof of correctness if a property holds true.

The resonance fluctuations within the (39991) Iochroma family are analyzed using orbital data from 396 co-orbital objects, spanning a semi-major axis range of 3.53 to 3.70 AU. This analysis reveals that the resonance structure is notably complex, featuring a potential maximum of 31 libration centers and 121 circulations within the defined boundaries. Libration centers dominate this landscape, accounting for approximately 76% of dynamics sites, while circulations represent about 24%. The mean circulatory width is estimated at 0.0012 ± 0.0001 in units of mean motion, and the primary location for these dynamics is centered around 3.62 ± 0.02 AU. Furthermore, a secondary population of circulations is identified, with a mean distance of 3.58 ± 0.02 AU from semi-major axis.

The current work extends this result to establish a similar linear combination formula for an arbitrary finite sequence of zeta values, without the alternating factor. The derivation relies primarily on the analytic properties of the Hurwitz zeta function.
